Article Title: Lung cancer deaths down 16% with low-dose CT screening: IARC
Article Text:
Lung cancer deaths can be reduced through low-dose CT screening, which can also help detect the disease before it reaches advanced stages in people at high risk, according to an IARC assessment.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Low-dose computed tomography (CT) screening can cut the risk of dying from lung cancer by 16% in high-risk people, while also reducing the incidence of advanced stage III or IV disease, an International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) working group has found.Published in The New England Journal of Medicine, the assessment found established evidence that low-dose CT reduces lung cancer mortality when used in people at high risk based mainly on age and smoking history.IARC convened a working group of 23 clinicians and scientists from 17 countries, including Dr Abhishek Shankar of All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi, to assess the benefits and harms of lung cancer screening.The evidence mainly applies to people aged 50 to 80 with a substantial smoking history, typically at least 20 to 30 pack-years. Studies involving former smokers generally included those who had quit within the previous 10 to 15 years, with screening usually performed annually.In India, people aged 50 to 80 with at least 20 pack-years of smoking who are current smokers or quit within the past 15 years can contact the Indian Lung Screening Trial, led by Dr Abhishek Shankar at AIIMS, New Delhi, about screening.Dr Shankar has invited eligible people to contact him for screening under the trial.The evidence behind the finding came mainly from randomised trials. In the US National Lung Screening Trial, people screened with low-dose CT had a 16% lower relative risk of dying from lung cancer than those screened with chest X-rays at seven years. The European NELSON trial also found lower lung cancer mortality among men screened with low-dose CT at 10 years.Based on this evidence, the IARC group classified low-dose CT as Group A, indicating established evidence that it reduces lung cancer mortality and the incidence of stage III or IV disease. Chest X-rays, with or without sputum examination, were classified as Group C, as their ability to reduce lung cancer mortality could not be established.However, the review cautioned that low-dose CT screening is not meant for everyone. False-positive results ranged from 1% to 42% across studies, depending on the screening protocol. Among those with false-positive results, 5% to 32% underwent at least one invasive procedure, with complications occurring in 10% to 22% of such procedures.The review also estimated that 3% to 26% of lung cancers detected in randomised trials involving high-risk people could represent overdiagnosis, meaning cancers that might not have caused harm during the person's lifetime.The working group said effective lung cancer screening needs more than CT scanners, including systems for identifying eligible people, assessing risk, monitoring nodules, providing treatment and follow-up, along with smoking-cessation support. Organised programmes also require trained staff, quality assurance, adequate healthcare capacity and equitable access.
Article Summary: Low-dose computed tomography (CT) screening can cut the risk of dying from lung cancer by 16% in high-risk people. It can also reduce the incidence of advanced stage III or IV disease, according to an IARC assessment. The evidence mainly applies to people aged 50 to 80 with a substantial smoking history.

Article Title: Jason and Kylie Kelce’s latest $2.9 billion market move marks a new milestone as their investment reaches 5,000+ stores
Article Text:
Jason and Kylie Kelce’s latest $2.9 billion market move marks a new milestone as their investment reaches 5,000+ stores

Jason Kelce backs a brand he already knew well

New Heights

Hank Sauce has already reached more than 5,000 stores

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Jason Kelce is expanding his post-NFL business portfolio, with his latest move taking him into the growing hot sauce market. Through Winnie Capital, the family office supporting the business and philanthropic activities of Jason and Kylie Kelce, a strategic equity investment has been made in Hank Sauce, the Sea Isle City, New Jersey-based brand that has grown from a local favorite into a product sold in thousands of stores. The deal gives Hank Sauce another major name behind its plans for wider national distribution while also adding a growing consumer brand to the Kelces’ business interests.Hank Sauce announced the strategic equity investment from Winnie Capital on December 22, 2025. Neither side disclosed the financial terms, meaning the amount invested and the size of the equity stake remain private.Jason Kelce’s connection to Hank Sauce, however, goes beyond the investment. The former Philadelphia Eagles center has spent considerable time around South Jersey over the years and was already familiar with Hank Sauce and its Sea Isle City restaurant before the business relationship developed.According to reporting surrounding the deal, Winnie Capital formally connected with the Hank Sauce founders in September 2024. That eventually developed into the investment announced more than a year later.This distinction is important. Kelce is not simply appearing in an advertising campaign for the company. Winnie Capital has taken an equity position in the existing business, while Jason is also expected to contribute to brand awareness, content and marketing as Hank Sauce attempts to reach a larger audience.Kylie Kelce is connected to the deal through Winnie Capital, which serves as the family office for the couple’s business and philanthropic activities. The announcement does not disclose a separate personal investment from Kylie, so her role is more accurately described through the family’s investment operation.Jason Kelce also brings something that cannot be measured simply by the undisclosed investment figure. After 13 NFL seasons with the Eagles and a growing media career that includes thepodcast with Travis Kelce, he has an audience that can introduce Hank Sauce to consumers far beyond its Jersey Shore base.Winnie Capital is investing in a company that has already spent years building its business.Brian “Hank” Ruxton, Matt Pittaluga and Josh Jaspan founded Hank Sauce in 2011. The business started on a much smaller scale before gradually expanding its production, restaurant operation and retail distribution.Hank Sauce now says its products are available in more than 5,000 retail locations nationwide. Its distribution includes retailers such as Publix, GIANT, ACME, ShopRite, Sprouts, Cabela’s and Ace Hardware, giving the company a footprint that already stretches well beyond New Jersey.The business also operates from a 10,000-square-foot manufacturing facility in Millville, New Jersey, a major change from its early years when production was considerably smaller and bottles were made by hand.Its Sea Isle City restaurant, meanwhile, dates back to 2012 and remains an important part of the company’s connection to the Jersey Shore.The product itself was built around a straightforward idea. Rather than competing only on extreme heat, Hank Sauce has focused heavily on flavor. That approach has allowed the company to appeal to customers who enjoy hot sauce without necessarily looking for the hottest product possible.Winnie Capital investment comes as Hank Sauce targets a much bigger marketHank Sauce is trying to expand in a sizeable category. The U.S. hot sauce market has been valued at roughly $2.9 billion, according to market figures cited in reporting surrounding Kelce’s investment.The opportunity for Hank Sauce is therefore much larger than its original Jersey Shore customer base.The company already has several pieces needed for further expansion, including its own production facility, more than 5,000 retail locations, an established product lineup and over a decade of operating history. The next challenge is increasing national recognition while continuing to add retailers, restaurants and other distribution channels.That is where Winnie Capital’s investment and Jason Kelce’s involvement could play a role. Along with providing capital, the partnership is expected to include work around content, marketing and brand visibility.For Kylie Kelce, the deal is connected to the broader activities of the family office she shares with Jason Kelce rather than a separately announced personal investment. For Jason Kelce, it gives him an equity interest through Winnie Capital in a company he was already familiar with as a consumer.Hank Sauce has now been operating for around 15 years, has expanded into more than 5,000 stores and produces its sauces from a 10,000-square-foot New Jersey facility. With Winnie Capital now holding an equity stake, the next stage of the company’s story will center on whether a brand built along the Jersey Shore can turn that existing footprint into a much larger national presence.
Article Summary: Hank Sauce announced the strategic equity investment from Winnie Capital on December 22, 2025. Neither side disclosed the financial terms, meaning the amount invested and the size of the equity stake remain private. The U.S. hot sauce market has been valued at roughly $2.9 billion, according to market figures.

Article Title: India's Essar Group to invest $15 billion in 'largest' US steel plant, Trump announces
Article Text:
President Donald Trump speaks as from right, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Energy Secretary Chris Wright, Essar Capital Director Prashant Ruia, Mesabi Metallics Chairman Rewant Ruia and Mesabi Metallics CEO Joe Broking

Project to link

Minnesota iron ore mine

with

Iowa steel plant

US President Donald Trump on Tuesday announced plans by Indian conglomerate Essar Group, through its US subsidiary Mesabi Metallics, to invest about $15 billion in a major steel plant in Iowa.Trump made the announcement at the White House alongside Essar Group co-founder Ravi Ruia and Mesabi Metallics chairman Rewant Ruia, describing the project as the largest steel plant in American history."Today we're thrilled to announce that Mesabi Metallics will be building the largest steel plant in American history in the great state of Iowa. It's the largest plant, one of the largest plants in the world, but it's the largest plant in America by far," Trump told reporters.The facility is expected to produce 10 million tonnes of steel a year once fully operational, with production targeted to begin in 2030. The project is also expected to create thousands of jobs during construction and nearly 2,000 permanent positions across the steel and mining operations.The Iowa plant will form part of an integrated US supply chain, with iron ore sourced from a new mine being developed by Mesabi Metallics in Minnesota's Mesabi Iron Range.The company has invested about $2.5 billion in the mine, which is expected to produce around 7.5 million tonnes of iron annually and create about 350 jobs.Rewant Ruia said he was born in India but had studied in New York, Boston and California, adding that he had spent half his life in the US and described the investment as "a true homecoming". He said the project would establish a fully integrated supply chain "from mine to mill".Trump highlighted the domestic nature of the operation, saying the Minnesota mine would be "the first new iron ore mine in the United States in more than 50 years with the highest quality ore.""In other words, this steel will be mined, melted, and made right here in the USA, which is something very unusual," Trump said.Rewant Ruia thanked the president "for bringing back the importance of building things in America." He also said the plant would use advanced technology and "will compete head-to-head with any steel plant in the world on size, quality and on cost."Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick attributed the investment partly to the administration's steel tariffs. Trump said companies were building in the US "because they don't want to pay tariffs".
Article Summary: Indian conglomerate Essar Group to invest about $15 billion in a major steel plant in Iowa. The facility is expected to produce 10 million tonnes of steel a year once fully operational, with production targeted to begin in 2030. The Iowa plant will form part of an integrated US supply chain, with iron ore sourced from a new mine in Minnesota.

Article Title: Father left $21 million in a charitable fund; son sought a $1 million donation but his access was cut off by the foundation
Article Text:
Philip Peterson, left, with his father Gordon in 2015. Image Credit: CNBC

How did the $21 million fund become the subject of a lawsuit

What changed between Peterson and WaterStone

WaterStone is based in northeast Colorado Springs. Image Credit: The Gazette

$1 million donation at the centre of the dispute

What does the lawsuit say about control of donor-advised funds

The case could clarify duties and rights of successor advisers and sponsors

A $21 million charitable fund is at the centre of a legal dispute after Philip Peterson, the son of its founder, alleged that WaterStone cut off his access and stopped acting on his recommendations. The fund was created by Gordon Peterson in 2005 for Christian charitable causes, and Philip became its sole successor adviser after his mother died. According to the lawsuit, the dispute escalated in 2024, when access to the account was revoked and a proposed $1 million donation was not processed. The case is now examining how much authority successor advisers actually have over donor-advised funds.Gordon Peterson established the Peterson Family Stewardship Fund with WaterStone in 2005. The fund was intended to support evangelical Christian charitable purposes. WaterStone, the name used by Christian Community Foundation, became responsible for holding and administering the money.According to MinistryWatch , Gordon died in 2019. His wife Ruth and son Philip had been recognised as advisers to the family fund from 2017. When Ruth died in 2021, Philip became the sole successor adviser. For several years, WaterStone continued to process the charitable grants he recommended.The fund was worth more than $21 million by the end of 2023, according to the lawsuit. CNBC reported that Peterson had continued to make recommendations from the account until the relationship with WaterStone deteriorated in 2024. At that point, he says, his access to information about the fund was cut off.The disagreement appears to have centred on how the fund would be managed and distributed in the future. CNBC reported that Peterson disagreed with WaterStone over a proposal concerning the fund's principal and investment income. He subsequently raised the possibility of moving the fund to another sponsor.According to MinistryWatch, Peterson says a March 5, 2024 Zoom call with WaterStone chief executive Ken Harrison ended with Peterson being told that further communication with the organisation would cease. Peterson then tried to restore access and contacted board members, but says those efforts did not resolve the dispute.The lawsuit alleges that WaterStone revoked his online access, suspended his advisory privileges and stopped processing his grant recommendations. Foley & Lardner reported that Peterson also alleges WaterStone refused to provide information about the account and directed him to stop contacting the organisation.One of the most significant recommendations involved a proposed $1 million grant to Operation Mobilization, a Christian missionary organisation that had previously received support from the Peterson family fund.MinistryWatch reported that Peterson says WaterStone denied the distribution after previously approving and administering his recommendations. It also reported that the fund made no charitable grants in 2024, according to the lawsuit.The issue was particularly important to Peterson because Operation Mobilization had a history of receiving support from his family. His lawsuit argues that WaterStone's actions interfered with the charitable purpose for which his father had established the fund.In February 2025, WaterStone agreed to make $400,000 in distributions, according to MinistryWatch. Peterson accepted those distributions but also raised concerns that the fund was still behind on charitable contributions from earlier years.The case raises a broader issue because a donor-advised fund does not work like a personal bank account for charitable giving. Once money is contributed, the sponsoring organisation legally controls the assets, while the donor or successor adviser can recommend where grants should go.Foley & Lardner explained that this distinction is central to this case. The law firm said WaterStone's sponsorship agreement gives it ultimate control and discretion over the fund and states that the original donor irrevocably gave up ownership and other rights to the contributions. That arrangement is common to donor-advised funds. The adviser can have an important role in suggesting charitable grants, but the sponsor retains legal control over the money.Peterson's lawsuit seeks more than the payment of one disputed grant. According to MinistryWatch, he is asking for an accounting of the fund, clarification of the rights and duties between himself and WaterStone, and an order requiring the organisation to carry out its responsibilities, including recommended grants. He is also seeking to transfer the fund to another organisation.Foley & Lardner reports that the case could clarify whether advisory rights that donors and successor advisers commonly rely upon are legally enforceable. WaterStone has argued in its motion to dismiss that it is not contractually required to follow Peterson's recommendations because the sponsorship agreement leaves ultimate authority with WaterStone.The case reaches beyond the Peterson family. It could help clarify what happens when a donor-advised fund sponsor and a successor adviser no longer agree about how charitable money should be handled.
Article Summary: Philip Peterson, the son of the fund's founder, alleges that WaterStone cut off his access and stopped acting on his recommendations. The dispute escalated in 2024, when access to the account was revoked and a proposed $1 million donation was not processed. The case is now examining how much authority successor advisers have over donor-advised funds.
